ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::0: For several decades, regulatory testing schemes for genetic damage have been standardized where the tests being utilized examined mutations and structural and numerical chromosomal damage. This has served the genetic toxicity community well when most of the substances being tested were amenable to such assays. The outcome from this testing is usually a dichotomous (yes/no) evaluation of test results, and in many instances, the information is only used to determine whether a substance has carcinogenic potential or not. Over the same time period, mechanisms and modes of action (MOAs) that elucidate a wider range of genomic damage involved in many adverse health outcomes have been recognized. In addition, a paradigm shift in applied genetic toxicology is moving the field toward a more quantitative dose-response analysis and point-of-departure (PoD) determination with a focus on risks to exposed humans. This is directing emphasis on genomic damage that is likely to induce changes associated with a variety of adverse health outcomes. This paradigm shift is moving the testing emphasis for genetic damage from a hazard identification only evaluation to a more comprehensive risk assessment approach that provides more insightful information for decision makers regarding the potential risk of genetic damage to exposed humans. To enable this broader context for examining genetic damage, a next generation testing strategy needs to take into account a broader, more flexible approach to testing, and ultimately modeling, of genomic damage as it relates to human exposure. This is consistent with the larger risk assessment context being used in regulatory decision making. As presented here, this flexible approach for examining genomic damage focuses on testing for relevant genomic effects that can be, as best as possible, associated with an adverse health effect. The most desired linkage for risk to humans would be changes in loci associated with human diseases, whether in somatic or germ cells. The outline of a flexible approach and associated considerations are presented in a series of nine steps, some of which can occur in parallel, which was developed through a collaborative effort by leading genetic toxicologists from academia, government, and industry through the International Life Sciences Institute (ILSI) Health and Environmental Sciences Institute (HESI) Genetic Toxicology Technical Committee (GTTC). The ultimate goal is to provide quantitative data to model the potential risk levels of substances, which induce genomic damage contributing to human adverse health outcomes. Any good risk assessment begins with asking the appropriate risk management questions in a planning and scoping effort. This step sets up the problem to be addressed (e.g., broadly, does genomic damage need to be addressed, and if so, how to proceed). The next two steps assemble what is known about the problem by building a knowledge base about the substance of concern and developing a rational biological argument for why testing for genomic damage is needed or not. By focusing on the risk management problem and potential genomic damage of concern, the next step of assay(s) selection takes place. The work-up of the problem during the earlier steps provides the insight to which assays would most likely produce the most meaningful data. This discussion does not detail the wide range of genomic damage tests available, but points to types of testing systems that can be very useful. Once the assays are performed and analyzed, the relevant data sets are selected for modeling potential risk. From this point on, the data are evaluated and modeled as they are for any other toxicology endpoint. Any observed genomic damage/effects (or genetic event(s)) can be modeled via a dose-response analysis and determination of an estimated PoD. When a quantitative risk analysis is needed for decision making, a parallel exposure assessment effort is performed (exposure assessment is not detailed here as this is not the focus of this discussion; guidelines for this assessment exist elsewhere). Then the PoD for genomic damage is used with the exposure information to develop risk estimations (e.g., using reference dose (RfD), margin of exposure (MOE) approaches) in a risk characterization and presented to risk managers for informing decision making. This approach is applicable now for incorporating genomic damage results into the decision-making process for assessing potential adverse outcomes in chemically exposed humans and is consistent with the ILSI HESI Risk Assessment in the 21st Century (RISK21) roadmap. This applies to any substance to which humans are exposed, including pharmaceuticals, agricultural products, food additives, and other chemicals. It is time for regulatory bodies to incorporate the broader knowledge and insights provided by genomic damage results into the assessments of risk to more fully understand the potential of adverse outcomes in chemically exposed humans, thus improving the assessment of risk due to genomic damage. The historical use of genomic damage data as a yes/no gateway for possible cancer risk has been too narrowly focused in risk assessment. The recent advances in assaying for and understanding genomic damage, including eventually epigenetic alterations, obviously add a greater wealth of information for determining potential risk to humans. Regulatory bodies need to embrace this paradigm shift from hazard identification to quantitative analysis and to incorporate the wider range of genomic damage in their assessments of risk to humans. The quantitative analyses and methodologies discussed here can be readily applied to genomic damage testing results now. Indeed, with the passage of the recent update to the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) in the US, the new generation testing strategy for genomic damage described here provides a regulatory agency (here the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), but suitable for others) a golden opportunity to reexamine the way it addresses risk-based genomic damage testing (including hazard identification and exposure). The framework supports better integration of mechanistic data into regulatory science. Implementation will require training programs for regulatory scientists and risk assessors. International harmonization of these approaches would benefit global chemical safety efforts. Environ. Mol. Mutagen. 58:264-283, 2017. © 2016 The Authors. Environmental and Molecular Mutagenesis Published by Wiley Periodicals, Inc.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::1: Nutritional supplements may improve development of infants born small (preterm or small for gestational age [SGA]) but may increase the risk of later metabolic disease. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the effects of macronutrient supplements for infants born small on later development and metabolism. We searched OvidMedline, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews from inception to April 1, 2019. Additional searches included controlled-trials.com, clinicaltrials.gov, and anzctr.org.au registries. Randomised or quasirandomised trials were included if the intention was to increase macronutrient intake to improve growth or development of infants born small. Studies had to assess post-discharge outcomes to meet inclusion criteria. Co-primary outcomes were cognitive impairment and metabolic risk. These outcomes were evaluated in toddlers (<3 years), childhood (3 to 8 years), and adolescence (9 to 18 years). Two reviewers independently extracted data from eligible studies. Quality was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Data were pooled using random-effect models for meta-analysis. Twenty-one randomised and one quasirandomised trial involving 3,680 infants were included. The included trials showed variable methodological quality across studies. In toddlers born small, supplementation did not alter cognitive impairment (relative risk [RR] 1.00; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.67 to 1.49; P = 0.99). Cognitive scores showed no differences between supplemented and unsupplemented groups (mean difference [MD] 0.57; 95% CI -0.71 to 1.84; P = 0.38). Motor scores similarly revealed no significant differences (MD 1.16; 95% CI -0.32 to 2.65; P = 0.12). However, fewer supplemented children had motor impairment (RR 0.76; 95% CI 0.62 to 0.94; P = 0.01). Subgroup analyses revealed supplementation improved cognitive scores in boys (MD 5.60; 95% CI 1.07 to 10.14; P = 0.02). Girls born small showed no cognitive benefit from supplementation (MD -2.04; 95% CI -7.04 to 2.95; P = 0.42). The subgroup of children born SGA demonstrated no alterations in cognitive or motor scores with supplementation. In childhood, cognitive impairment rates were similar between groups (RR 0.81; 95% CI 0.26 to 2.57; P = 0.72). Cognitive scores in childhood showed no significant differences (MD 1.02; 95% CI -1.91 to 3.95; P = 0.50). Blood pressure measurements revealed no differences between supplemented and unsupplemented groups (P > 0.05). Triglyceride concentrations were similar across both groups (P > 0.05). Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) levels showed no significant differences (P > 0.05). Supplemented children had lower fasting glucose levels (mmol/L: MD -0.20; 95% CI -0.34 to -0.06; P = 0.005). High-density lipoprotein (HDL) concentrations were higher in supplemented children (mmol/L: MD 0.11; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.19; P = 0.02). Subgroup analyses found no evidence of blood pressure differences in boys or girls born small. SGA children similarly showed no blood pressure differences between supplemented and unsupplemented groups. In adolescence, blood pressure measurements were comparable between groups (P > 0.05). Triglyceride levels in adolescence showed no significant differences (P > 0.05). LDL and HDL concentrations were similar between supplemented and unsupplemented adolescents (P > 0.05). Fasting blood glucose levels revealed no differences in adolescence (P > 0.05). Insulin resistance measures were comparable across both groups (P > 0.05). Fasting insulin concentrations showed no significant differences (P > 0.05). Study limitations include considerable unexplained heterogeneity across trials. The overall quality of evidence ranged from low to very low. Limited data availability beyond early childhood represents another important limitation. Early macronutrient supplementation for infants born small did not alter later cognitive function based on randomised trial evidence. Some evidence suggests supplementation may decrease motor impairment specifically in toddlers. Observational studies have reported different findings regarding metabolic outcomes. Randomised trial evidence indicates early macronutrient supplementation improves some metabolic outcomes in childhood. The study registration number is CRD42019127858.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::2: Objectives Recently, two point-of-care (PoC) feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) antibody test kits (Witness and Anigen Rapid) were reported as being able to differentiate FIV-vaccinated from FIV-infected cats at a single time point, irrespective of the gap between testing and last vaccination (0-7 years). The aim of the current study was to investigate systematically anti-FIV antibody production over time in response to the recommended primary FIV vaccination series. Methods First, residual plasma from the original study was tested using a laboratory-based ELISA to determine whether negative results with PoC testing were due to reduced as opposed to absent antibodies to gp40. Second, a prospective study was performed using immunologically naive client-owned kittens and cats given a primary FIV vaccination series using a commercially available inactivated whole cell/inactivated whole virus vaccine (Fel-O-Vax FIV, three subcutaneous injections at 4 week intervals). These animals were tested systematically up to 11 times over 6 months using four commercially available PoC FIV antibody kits. The SNAP FIV/FeLV Combo kit detects antibodies to p15/p24 viral proteins. Witness FeLV/FIV targets gp40 envelope protein specifically. Anigen Rapid FIV/FeLV identifies both p24 and gp40 antibodies simultaneously. VetScan FeLV/FIV Rapid focuses exclusively on p24 detection. Results The laboratory-based ELISA showed cats from the original study vaccinated within the previous 0-15 months had detectable levels of antibodies to gp40, despite testing negative with two kits that use gp40 as a capture antigen (Witness and Anigen Rapid kits). The prospective study showed that antibody testing with SNAP Combo and VetScan Rapid was positive in all cats 2 weeks after the second primary FIV vaccination. These two tests remained positive for the duration of the study, with 12/12 cats positive using SNAP Combo and 10/12 cats positive using VetScan Rapid. Antibody testing with Witness and Anigen Rapid was also positive in a high proportion of cats 2 weeks after the second primary FIV vaccination, showing 8/12 and 7/12 positive results respectively. However, antibody levels declined below the level of detection in most cats by 1 month after the third (final) primary FIV vaccination, affecting 10/12 animals. All cats tested negative using Witness and Anigen Rapid 6 months after the third primary FIV vaccination. Conclusions and relevance This study has shown that a primary course of FIV vaccination does not interfere with FIV antibody testing in cats using Witness and Anigen Rapid, provided primary vaccination has not occurred within the previous 6 months. Consequently, Witness and Anigen Rapid antibody test kits can be used reliably to determine FIV infection status at the time of annual booster FIV vaccination to help detect 'vaccine breakthroughs'. These kits are also suitable for cats that have not received a primary course of FIV vaccination within the preceding 6 months. The duration of antibody response following annual booster FIV vaccination and the resulting effect on antibody testing using PoC kits needs to be determined by further research. The mechanism(s) for the variation in FIV antibody test kit performance remains unclear.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::3: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a rare monogenic disorder characterized by benign tumors in multiple organs as well as a high prevalence of epilepsy, intellectual disability and autism. TSC is caused by inactivating mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes. Heterozygocity induces hyperactivation of mTOR which can be inhibited by mTOR inhibitors, such as rapamycin, which have proven efficacy in the treatment of TSC-associated symptoms. The present study aimed to identify molecular changes associated with social and cognitive deficits in the brain tissue of Tsc1 +/- mice. A second objective was to investigate the molecular effects of rapamycin treatment, which has been shown to ameliorate genotype-related behavioural deficits. A quantitative mass spectrometry-based shotgun proteomic approach (LC-MS E ) was employed as an unbiased method to detect changes in protein levels. Changes identified in the initial profiling stage were validated using selected reaction monitoring (SRM). Protein Set Enrichment Analysis was employed to identify dysregulated pathways. LC-MS E analysis of Tsc1 +/- mice and controls ( n = 30) identified 51 proteins changed in frontal cortex and 108 in the hippocampus. LC-MS E analysis was also employed on Tsc1 +/- and wildtype mice ( n = 34) treated with rapamycin or vehicle. Rapamycin treatment exerted a stronger proteomic effect in Tsc1 +/- mice with significant changes, mainly decreased expression, observed in 231 and 106 proteins, respectively. The cellular compartments "myelin sheet" and "neurofilaments" were affected by rapamycin treatment. Thirty-three proteins which were altered in Tsc1 +/- mice were normalized following rapamycin treatment. These normalized proteins included oxidative stress related proteins, myelin-specific proteins and ribosomal proteins. ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::4: Silica nanoparticles (nanoSiO 2 ) are promising systems that can deliver biologically active compounds to tissues such as the heart in a controllable manner. However, cardiac toxicity induced by nanoSiO 2 has been recently related to abnormal calcium handling and energetic failure in cardiomyocytes. The precise mechanisms underlying this energetic debacle remain unclear and require systematic investigation. This article explores the ex vivo heart function and mitochondria after exposure to nanoSiO 2 to elucidate these mechanisms. The cumulative administration of nanoSiO 2 reduced the mechanical performance index of the rat heart with a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC 50 ) of 93 μg/mL. The relaxation rate was specifically affected by nanoparticle exposure. In isolated mitochondria nanoSiO 2 was found to be internalized through direct observation. Oxidative phosphorylation was inhibited by the internalized nanoparticles. The mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨ m ) was significantly reduced following nanoSiO 2 treatment. The mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) was induced with an increasing dose of nanoSiO 2 . Cyclosporine A (CsA), a potent blocker of the mPTP, partially recovered the pore dysfunction. The activity of aconitase was reduced due to nanoSiO 2 exposure. Thiol oxidation in the adenine nucleotide translocase was also diminished by nanoparticle treatment. These findings suggest that nanoSiO 2 induces the mPTP via thiol modification. ROS generation appears to be another pathway through which nanoSiO 2 triggers mPTP opening. In cardiac cells exposed to nanoSiO 2 , enhanced viability was observed after application of MitoTEMPO, a specific mitochondrial antioxidant. Reduction of H 2 O 2 levels accompanied the improved cell survival with MitoTEMPO treatment. CsA treatment in adult rat cardiac cells reduced the nanoSiO 2 -triggered cell death significantly. ATP production recovered from 32.4 to 65.4% following CsA administration. Evaluation of the mitochondrial effect of nanoSiO 2 was performed in human cardiomyocytes to confirm cross-species relevance. A 40% inhibition of maximal oxygen consumption rate in mitochondria was observed at 500 μg/mL in human cells. A remarkable diminution in the spare respiratory capacity was identified under this condition. This indicates reduced availability of extra ATP during sudden increases in energy demand. Increased LDH release was found at elevated doses of nanoSiO 2 in human cardiomyocytes. Necrosis reached 48% at the highest nanoparticle concentrations tested. LDH levels peaked at 85% under maximal exposure conditions. CsA application partially prevented these deleterious effects in human cardiac cells. Exposure to nanoSiO 2 affects cardiac function via mitochondrial dysfunction through mPTP opening. Reducing ROS can partially avoid the aforementioned effects. Retarding the opening of the mPTP represents an alternative protective strategy. These novel cardioprotective strategies could be considered as potential therapies to decrease the side effects of nanoSiO 2 exposure in clinical applications.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::5: Return to play (RTP) of National Football League (NFL) athletes after isolated anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears has been reported. ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::6: Pulmonary hypertension in response to exercise is a marker of the hemodynamic severity of mitral stenosis (MS). Peak exercise SPAP adds incremental prognostic value beyond resting parameters for risk stratification in mitral stenosis patients.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::7: The relationship between chronic liver disease and COVID-19 patient outcomes remains poorly understood. Our investigation focused on determining whether liver conditions influence mortality rates in hospitalized COVID-19 cases. Statistical models calculated adjusted odds ratios to quantify relationships between liver pathology, alcohol-related disorders, invasive respiratory support, and thirty-day hospital death rates. Our cohort included 259,110 individuals with a median age of 70 years and an interquartile range spanning 54 to 83 years. Male patients constituted 52% of the study population. Chronic liver disease was documented in 15,476 patients, representing 6.0% of admissions. Alcohol use disorders affected 10,006 patients, accounting for 3.9% of the cohort. Overall mortality reached 38,203 deaths, corresponding to a 15% fatality rate. Among mechanically ventilated patients, 7,475 deaths occurred, yielding a 28% mortality rate in this subgroup. Patients with chronic liver disease experienced 2,941 deaths, translating to a 19% mortality rate. Chronic liver disease overall showed adjusted odds ratios of 1.54 for mechanical ventilation and 1.79 for thirty-day mortality, both highly significant. Mild hepatic disease demonstrated protective associations, with odds ratios of 0.55 for ventilation and 0.54 for death. Compensated cirrhosis yielded odds ratios of 0.64 for mechanical ventilation and 0.71 for mortality. Decompensated cirrhosis patients had an odds ratio of 0.65 for receiving ventilation but 2.21 for dying. Primary hepatocellular carcinoma showed an odds ratio of 0.34 for ventilation access yet 1.38 for death. Alcohol use disorders produced odds ratios of 0.82 for mechanical ventilation and 1.11 for mortality. Chronic viral hepatitis showed no significant association with COVID-19 death. Non-viral, non-alcoholic chronic hepatitis similarly demonstrated no mortality association. Organ transplant recipients, including those with liver grafts, showed no elevated death risk. Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome did not predict COVID-19 mortality in our analysis. These findings suggest that treatment limitation policies may have influenced outcomes. Specifically, patients with decompensated cirrhosis, primary liver cancer, or alcohol disorders received less aggressive respiratory support despite higher mortality. French clinical practices during 2020 may have incorporated prognostic liver factors into ventilator allocation decisions. Such rationing could explain the paradoxical pattern of reduced ventilation access coupled with increased death rates in specific liver disease subgroups.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::8: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) has led to a significant number of mortalities worldwide. The clinical manifestations of COVID-19 are diverse and severe and 20% of infected patients are reported to be in a critical condition. A loss in lung function and pulmonary fibrosis are the main manifestations of patients with the severe form of the disease. The lung function is affected, even after recovery, thereby greatly affecting the psychology and well-being of patients. Participants must meet the following simultaneous inclusion criteria: over 18 years of age, should have recovered from severe or critical COVID-19 cases, should exhibit pulmonary fibrosis after recovery, and should exhibit Qi-Yin deficiency syndrome as indicated in the system of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM). The eligible candidates will be randomized into treatment or control groups. The treatment group will receive modern medicine (pirfenidone) plus TCM whereas the control group will be administered modern medicine plus TCM placebo. The lung function index will be continuously surveyed and recorded. By comparing the treatment effect between the two groups, the study intends to explore whether TCM can improve the effectiveness of modern medicine in patients with pulmonary fibrosis arising as a sequelae after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Some studies reveal that pirfenidone leads to a delay in the decline of forced expiratory vital capacity. This medication has been shown to reduce mortality rates in affected populations. TCM has been proven to be efficacious in treating pulmonary fibrosis through various mechanisms. However, its role in treating pulmonary fibrosis related to COVID-19 has not been explored. A multicenter, parallel-group, randomized controlled, interventional, prospective clinical trial has been designed to address this knowledge gap. The trial will determine if a new comprehensive treatment for pulmonary fibrosis related to COVID-19 is feasible. Patient quality of life improvements will be measured as a key outcome. This trial was registered at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2000033284) on 26th May 2020. The registration occurred prospectively before patient enrollment began. Multiple medical centers across different regions will participate in data collection. The study protocol received ethical approval from institutional review boards at all participating sites.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::9: Temperature and water availability are two of the most important variables affecting all aspects of an anuran's key physiological processes such as body temperature (T b), evaporative water loss (EWL) and standard metabolic rate (SMR). Since anurans display pronounced sexual dimorphism, evidence suggests that these processes are further influenced by other factors such as vapour pressure deficit (VPD), sex and body mass (M b). Few investigations have simultaneously examined multiple physiological responses across broad temperature gradients in species occupying different habitats. The present study therefore measured T b, whole-animal EWL and whole-animal SMR across ecologically relevant ambient temperatures (T a) in three African anuran species with contrasting lifestyles. We selected the principally aquatic African clawed frog (Xenopus laevis), the stream-breeding common river frog (Amietia delalandii), and the largely terrestrial raucous toad (Sclerophrys capensis) as our focal taxa. Wild-caught individuals were subjected to experimental trials at temperatures ranging from 5 to 35°C in 5°C increments. VPD proved a superior predictor of EWL rates compared to T a in two of the three species examined. All three physiological variables (T b, whole-animal EWL, and whole-animal SMR) exhibited positive relationships with increasing T a. Body mass influenced T b in A. delalandii and S. capensis, whereas X. laevis showed no such relationship. Only S. capensis demonstrated a significant positive effect of M b on whole-animal SMR. Within-species analyses revealed no significant effects of VPD, M b, or sex on whole-animal EWL. The aquatic specialist X. laevis was unique in showing no M b effects on any of the three physiological variables measured. These patterns indicate that body mass does not uniformly affect physiological responses across anuran taxa. Ecological specialisation may mediate how body mass influences physiological performance in amphibians. Aquatic species like X. laevis may experience different thermal and hydric constraints than terrestrial or semi-aquatic species. The buffering capacity of aquatic environments could reduce the physiological relevance of body mass variation. Consequently, researchers should interpret the role of M b within the framework of both physiological mechanisms and habitat-specific selective pressures. Future comparative studies must account for ecological context when evaluating morphological predictors of amphibian physiology.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::10: Chronotaraxis is an impairment of the perception of the sequencing of time. This alteration of temporality has been described as being characteristically associated with thalamic involvement, specifically in the dorsomedial nucleus. We report the clinical cases of two patients with acute ischaemic strokes located in said territory. The clinical presentation was based on this symptom as the predominant feature. Recognition of chronotaraxis proved essential in determining the therapeutic approach for both individuals. The first patient demonstrated profound disorientation regarding the order of recent events. The second patient exhibited similar difficulties in sequencing temporal information during clinical examination. In both instances, the perception of temporality served as the key diagnostic indicator of the ischaemic condition. Awareness and dissemination of this association may be vital in the management of patients with thalamic disorders. Early identification allows clinicians to initiate appropriate interventions before further neurological deterioration occurs. The possibility of influencing and modifying the initial approach represents a significant advantage in stroke management. Recognition of a specific symptom, such as chronotaraxis, can prevent the spread of thalamic damage to adjacent neural structures. Long-term sequelae can be minimized through prompt therapeutic intervention. Cognitive impairments constitute the most concerning complications of thalamic infarction. Memory consolidation deficits frequently accompany dorsomedial thalamic lesions. Executive function may also be compromised in patients with this anatomical localization of stroke. Attention and concentration difficulties often persist beyond the acute phase of illness. The thalamus serves as a critical relay station for multiple cortical networks involved in temporal processing. Disruption of these pathways produces the characteristic symptoms observed in chronotaraxis. Neuroimaging studies have confirmed the correlation between dorsomedial thalamic lesions and temporal sequencing deficits. Functional connectivity between the thalamus and prefrontal cortex appears particularly vulnerable to ischaemic injury. Rehabilitation strategies targeting temporal orientation may improve outcomes in affected patients. Cognitive training programs have shown promise in restoring some aspects of temporal perception. The prognosis varies depending on the extent of thalamic involvement and the timeliness of intervention. Early thrombolytic therapy may limit infarct size and preserve function. Multidisciplinary care teams provide optimal management for these complex neurological presentations.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::11: Some infectious diseases, such as influenza, tuberculosis, and SARS-CoV-2, may be transmitted when virus-laden particles expelled from an infectious person are inhaled by someone else, which is known as the airborne transmission route. These virus-laden particles are more concentrated in the expiratory jet of an infectious person than elsewhere in a well-mixed room. This near-field enhancement in virion exposure has not been well quantified in previous research. Transmission of airborne viruses depends on factors that are inherently variable and, in many cases, poorly constrained. Quantifying this uncertainty requires large ensembles of model simulations that span the variability in input parameters. Models that are well-suited to simulate the near-field evolution of respiratory particles are also computationally expensive. This computational cost limits the exploration of parametric uncertainty in transmission modeling. We developed the Quadrature-based model of Respiratory Aerosol and Droplets (QuaRAD) to perform many simulations spanning the wide variability in factors governing airborne transmission. QuaRAD is an efficient framework for simulating the evolution of virus-laden particles after they are expelled from an infectious person. The model also simulates deposition of particles to the nasal cavity of a susceptible person. QuaRAD calculates the subsequent risk of initial infection following particle deposition. We simulated 10,000 scenarios to quantify the risk of initial infection by SARS-CoV-2 specifically. The predicted risk of infection was highly variable among scenarios. In each scenario, infection risk was strongly enhanced near the infectious individual compared to far-field exposure. In more than 50% of scenarios, the physical distancing needed to avoid near-field enhancements in airborne transmission exceeded two meters. The recommended safe distance of two meters (six feet) was insufficient when the infectious person is not wearing a mask. The distance defining the near-field extent was highly variable among scenarios, ranging considerably across different conditions. The variability in the near-field extent is explained predominantly by variability in expiration velocity among individuals. Expiration velocity determines how far respiratory particles travel before dispersing into the room environment. Our findings suggest that maintaining at least two meters of distance from an infectious person greatly reduces exposure to airborne virions. Protections against airborne transmission, such as N95 respirators, should be available when distancing is not possible in practical settings.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::12: Open fractures are contaminated wounds that contain gram-positive and gram-negative organisms; therefore, wide-spectrum antibiotic therapy should be incorporated into the treatment plan. Antibiotics should be initiated as soon after injury as possible, preferably within 3 hours of injury, after which time the rate of infection has been reported to increase. Time to surgical debridement within 12 hours of injury has not been reported to affect the rate of infection, given that a patient is being treated with antibiotics. An antibiotic bead pouch and vacuum-assisted wound closure may help reduce the risk for secondary and nosocomial contamination and subsequent infection. Open fractures are always associated with a soft-tissue injury; therefore, they can be considered a soft-tissue injury that involves a fracture. The management of the bone and the soft tissues in a patient with an open fracture is the major determinant of fracture healing and functional restoration of the injured extremity. The formulation of a soft-tissue treatment plan must occur during the initial wound assessment and the initial fixation of an open fracture and should not be considered a secondary or consecutive process. A soft-tissue surgeon should be consulted the night of the injury. Selection of fracture fixation depends on the fractured bone, the location of the fracture (intra-articular, metaphyseal, or diaphyseal), the extent of soft-tissue injury and contamination, and the physiologic status of the patient. More than one fixation method may be applicable for the management of a specific injury; therefore, a surgeon's expertise and the availability of implants also should be considered. Surgeons must understand bone healing biology to achieve successful outcomes in the management of open fractures. The cornerstones of these bone healing treatments include optimization of host biology, recognition of a patient's nutritional status, appropriate use of medications, and eradication of infection. Surgeons should consider bone grafting and/or the use of biologics to achieve bony union in patients with an acute open fracture and in the management of delayed union or nonunion. Vascular assessment is critical in all open fracture cases to ensure adequate blood supply to the affected limb. Compartment syndrome remains a serious complication requiring immediate fasciotomy to prevent permanent tissue damage.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::13:
PURPOSE: Cyclical patterns of compliance have been observed with many health-related activities such as dieting and exercise. Whether such patterns exist among users of chronic medications remains unexplored. This study estimates the percentage of patients who restart osteoporosis therapy after a prolonged lapse in medication use. We also identify factors associated with a return to compliance after treatment interruption.

METHODS: We studied 26,636 new users of osteoporosis medications including alendronate, calcitonin, estrogen, raloxifene, or risedronate. All participants were age 65 or older at study entry. An extended lapse in refill compliance was defined as a period of at least 60 days after completing one prescription without obtaining any refill for osteoporosis medication. Survival curves estimated the length of time until therapy resumption occurred. Cox proportional hazards analysis assessed associations between patient characteristics and the rate of resuming treatment. A case crossover analysis examined whether certain events occurring during follow-up triggered a return to refill compliance.

RESULTS: Among patients who stopped therapy for at least 60 days, an estimated 30% restarted treatment within 6 months. Approximately 50% of these patients restarted within 2 years of their treatment gap. A subgroup of patients had at least 6 months of continuous use before their interruption in treatment (n=5863). In this subgroup, 42% restarted therapy within 6 months. Within 2 years, 59% of this subgroup had resumed medication use. Younger patients showed higher rates of returning after a break in medication use. Women were more likely to return compared to men. Those with a history of fracture demonstrated increased likelihood of treatment resumption. Recent hip fractures predicted a return to treatment during the follow-up period. Discharges from nursing homes also predicted treatment resumption. Bone mineral density testing was associated with patients restarting their medications.

CONCLUSION: Extended gaps in treatment are common among users of osteoporosis medications. The effectiveness of these drugs when used in an interrupted manner remains unknown. Compliance interventions should emphasize the need for continuous medication use. Further research must understand why patients often go for months without refilling prescriptions. Whether similar utilization patterns exist for other chronic medications requires additional investigation.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::14: Imbalances in the gut microbial community (dysbiosis) of vertebrates have been associated with several gastrointestinal and autoimmune diseases. The specific bacterial taxa that drive gut dysbiosis remain poorly characterized across different host species. Different anatomical regions of the gastrointestinal tract may exhibit varying degrees of vulnerability to microbial disruption. Developmental stages during early life could present critical windows when dysbiosis is more likely to establish. Non-model organisms have received insufficient research attention despite growing evidence that gut microbiota profoundly influence overall health outcomes. We examined microbiome alterations during dysbiosis across multiple gastrointestinal compartments in ostriches (Struthio camelus), which are long-lived birds experiencing substantial juvenile mortality. The study analyzed 16S rRNA gene sequences from ileum, cecum, and colon tissues collected from 68 individuals that succumbed to suspected enterocolitis within their first three months. Age-matched controls consisted of 50 healthy individuals that underwent euthanasia for comparative analysis. Longitudinal sampling of environmental sources and fecal material enabled identification of where pathogenic bacteria originated. Developmental timing of when dysbiosis-associated microbes first appeared could be determined through this temporal sampling approach. Diseased individuals exhibited dramatically reduced microbial alpha diversity compared to controls across all three gastrointestinal regions examined. Beta diversity patterns also showed substantial divergence between diseased and healthy birds throughout the entire gut. The inverse correlation between diversity and disease remained strong across all age groups specifically in the ileum. Cecum and colon tissues showed weakening associations between low diversity and disease as birds matured. Enterobacteriaceae, Peptostreptococcaceae, Porphyromonadaceae, and Clostridium genera showed positive associations with mortality outcomes. Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae, Erysipelotrichaceae, Turicibacter, and Roseburia taxa correlated with healthy status. Food sources showed no contamination with dysbiosis-associated bacterial lineages. Water supplies similarly lacked pathogenic microbial signatures. Soil substrate contained no detectable dysbiosis-related bacteria. Fecal samples collected repeatedly revealed that pathobionts colonized ostrich guts immediately following hatching. These opportunistic microbes underwent population expansion specifically in hosts harboring low overall microbial diversity. Mortality events occurred multiple weeks after initial pathobiont colonization. Understanding how pathobionts first enter neonatal hosts represents a crucial research priority. Determining which factors promote diverse microbiota establishment could illuminate dysbiosis prevention strategies and healthy development pathways.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::15: We investigate the reason for the quantum speedup -- quantum algorithms requiring fewer computation steps than their classical counterparts. We extend their representation to the process of setting the problem. The initial measurement selects a setting at random, Bob (the problem setter) unitarily changes it into the desired one. This representation is accessible to Bob and any external observer. Alice (the problem solver) cannot access this representation because it would reveal the function computed by the black box. The function must remain hidden inside the black box from Alice's perspective. We resort to relational quantum mechanics as our theoretical framework. To Alice, the projection of the quantum state due to the initial measurement is retarded at the end of her problem solving action. The algorithm input state remains one of complete ignorance of the setting from her viewpoint. Through black box computations, she unitarily sends this state into the output state. The output state encodes the corresponding solution for each possible setting. The final measurement acquires these solutions. We demonstrate that the final measurement can select any part -- say the R-th part -- of the random outcome of the initial measurement. This selection projects the input state to Alice on a state of lower entropy. In this lower entropy state, she knows a corresponding part of the problem setting. The quantum algorithm is a sum over classical histories. In each history, Alice knows in advance one of the R-th parts of the setting. She performs the black box computations still required to identify the solution in each history. This retrocausality model provides the number of black box computations required to solve an oracle problem for a given value of R. Conversely, the model yields the value of R that explains the speedup of a known quantum algorithm. Setting R = 1/2 always yields the number of black box computations required by an existing quantum algorithm. The same value provides the order of magnitude of the number required by an optimal algorithm.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::16: Cardiac disease and clinical intervention may both lead to an increased risk for thrombosis events due to modified blood flow in the heart, and thereby a change in the mechanical stimuli of blood cells passing through the chambers of the heart. Platelet activation levels depend on the magnitude and characteristics of mechanical stresses present in circulating blood. Our study focuses on computational analysis of left ventricular hemodynamics using patient-specific anatomical data. The Navier-Stokes equations govern the fluid dynamics within the ventricular chamber. Mitral valve flow is represented through a parameterized mathematical framework that captures the valve's opening geometry. Finite element discretization provides the numerical solution from which velocity and pressure fields are obtained. The velocity gradient tensor undergoes triple decomposition to isolate three distinct kinematic components. Rigid body rotation represents one mode of fluid motion in this decomposition scheme. Irrotational straining constitutes the second fundamental flow pattern. Shear deformation forms the third independent component of the velocity gradient. These three flow structures impose mechanically distinct stimuli on suspended blood cells. Simulations incorporating mitral valve clip intervention demonstrate substantial alterations in ventricular flow patterns. Quantitative comparison reveals differential responses among the three kinematic components following clip placement. Shear components exhibited disproportionately larger increases relative to rotational and strain components in clipped cases. One particular case showed a 64 percent reduction in effective valve opening area. This geometric change produced a 90 percent elevation in both rotation and strain magnitudes. The same intervention resulted in a 150 percent increase in shear magnitude, demonstrating non-proportional scaling. The disproportionate shear increase suggests specific mechanical activation pathways for platelets. Patient-specific computational workflows can simulate proposed interventions before clinical implementation. Detailed flow analysis provides quantitative metrics for comparing treatment options. Such computational frameworks could enhance risk stratification protocols for thrombotic complications. The methodology supports evidence-based clinical decision-making regarding cardiac interventions. Future applications may include optimization of device placement and sizing for individual patients.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::17: The diffuse very high-energy (VHE, > 100 GeV) gamma-ray emission observed in the central 200 pc of the Milky Way by H.E.S.S. was found to follow the dense matter distribution in the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) up to a longitudinal distance of about 130 pc to the Galactic Centre (GC), where the flux rapidly decreases. Recent sensitive H.E.S.S. analysis revealed that the cosmic-ray (CR) density profile drops with the distance to the centre, making data compatible with a steady cosmic PeVatron at the GC. In this paper, we extend this analysis to obtain for the first time a detailed characterisation of the correlation with matter and to search for additional features and individual gamma-ray sources in the inner 200 pc. Our study utilizes 250 hours of H.E.S.S. observational data combined with improved analysis techniques. We perform a detailed morphology study of the diffuse VHE emission observed from the GC ridge and reconstruct its total spectrum. The emission correlated with dense matter covers the full CMZ. The flux from matter-correlated emission represents approximately half the total diffuse emission flux measured. Some emission at higher latitude likely originates from hadronic collisions of CRs in less dense regions of the GC interstellar medium. An additional emission component centred on the GC extends over about 15 pc. This component is consistent with the existence of a strong CR density gradient. The presence of a CR accelerator at the very centre of our Galaxy is confirmed by these observations. The spectrum of the full ridge diffuse emission is compatible with the one previously derived from the central regions. A single population of particles fills the entire CMZ, as suggested by spectral consistency. We report the discovery of a VHE gamma-ray source near the GC radio arc. The newly discovered source is produced by the pulsar wind nebula candidate G0.13-0.11. This identification adds to the inventory of point sources in the Galactic Centre region and demonstrates the capability of current instruments to resolve discrete objects within complex diffuse backgrounds.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::18: These international clinical practice recommendations (CPR) for developmental coordination disorder (DCD), initiated by the European Academy of Childhood Disability (EACD), aim to address key questions on the definition, diagnosis, assessment, intervention, and psychosocial aspects of DCD relevant for clinical practice. The development process involved systematic literature reviews combined with formal expert consensus methods to answer key questions across five distinct areas. Literature searches on mechanisms, assessment, and intervention were updated to include all relevant studies published since the previous 2012 recommendations. Completely new literature searches were conducted specifically for psychosocial issues and for adolescents and adults with DCD, areas not comprehensively covered previously. The Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine framework was used to rate all evidence according to levels 1 through 4. Two face-to-face meetings brought together an international, multidisciplinary expert panel to discuss areas where research evidence was insufficient. Five additional Delphi rounds were completed to achieve consensus on good clinical practice recommendations where empirical data was lacking. The final document contains thirty-five recommendations in total. Eight recommendations derive directly from empirical evidence identified in the literature reviews, with three addressing assessment and five addressing intervention. Twenty-two recommendations represent updates or modifications of recommendations that appeared in the 2012 version. Two new good clinical practice recommendations address diagnosis and assessment procedures. Three new good clinical practice recommendations focus specifically on psychosocial issues affecting individuals with DCD. Active video games are now recommended as useful adjuncts to traditional activity-oriented and participation-oriented interventions, based on emerging evidence. Two recommendations specifically target adolescents and adults with DCD, a population previously underserved in clinical guidelines. The CPR-DCD provides clinicians and scientists from varied disciplines with comprehensive, current understanding of DCD. National healthcare systems can adapt these international recommendations to create country-specific guidelines. The guidelines represent the first international effort to provide evidence-based recommendations for adolescents and adults with this condition.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::19: Hypertension can lead to mood disorders that may worsen or ameliorate depending on the type of antihypertensive prescribed. Depression is associated with modifications in basal brain asymmetry particularly that of the frontal cortex, which is involved in blood pressure control. Different vasoactive drugs may change the brain's asymmetry in a manner that contributes to cognition status. We studied the bilateral activity of several neuropeptidases in frontal cortex as a reflect of the functional status of certain neuropeptides involved in mood. Using arylamide derivatives as substrates, we fluorometrically analysed the activity of these enzymes in the left and right frontal cortex of control untreated Wistar-Kyoto (WKY) and spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHRs). We compared their activities with WKY or SHR treated with the antihypertensive drugs captopril (CAP) and propranolol (PRO). Additional comparisons included animals treated with the hypertensive agent N (G)-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester. Systolic blood pressure (SBP) measurements were obtained from all experimental groups to confirm their cardiovascular status. Untreated WKY exhibited normotensive values of SBP as expected for this strain. WKY treated with CAP or PRO maintained normal blood pressure levels. SHR treated with CAP also exhibited normotensive values of SBP. WKY treated with N (G)-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester demonstrated hypertensive values of SBP. Untreated SHR showed elevated blood pressure consistent with their genetic background. SHR treated with PRO and N(G)-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester also demonstrated hypertensive values of SBP. Changes in the bilateral distribution of neuropeptidases depended on the strain, the enzyme analysed and the drug used. Normotensive WKY groups revealed intrahemispheric correlations mainly in the left hemisphere. WKY treated with N(G)-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester demonstrated intrahemispheric correlations mainly in the right hemisphere. SHR groups also showed correlations predominantly in the right hemisphere. Interhemispheric correlations were mostly observed in WKY groups. SHR groups with antihypertensive treatments (CAP, PRO) also exhibited interhemispheric correlations. Our results suggest specific brain bilateral patterns of neuropeptidase activities in WKY that change in SHR. This observation may be related to the cognitive disorders that have been described in these animals under antihypertensive or hypertensive drug treatments.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::20: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the value and efficacy of rapid response teams (RRTs) for different triggering events in total hip arthroplasty (THA) patients. A retrospective review of all RRT events at a single, tertiary referral center from 2014 to 2016 was performed. Inclusion criteria were defined as patients >18 years old that underwent primary or revision THA. Information queried included demographics, primary reason for RRT, Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), underlying etiology, whether any changes in management occurred, and whether the patient was uptriaged. In total, 168 RRTs were called on 153 hip arthroplasty patients (mean age 65.2 ± 14.1 years; mean body mass index 32.3 ± 4.8, 66% female). Length of stay in RRT for primary THA was 3.4 days. Revision THA patients requiring RRT stayed 6.2 days. Primary THA patients without RRT had a 2.4-day length of stay (P < .001). Revision THA patients not requiring RRT stayed 4.6 days (P = .005). There were no mortalities among any patients in the study cohort. RRTs for hypotension/presyncope (11%) resulted in significantly fewer changes in management (P < .01) than tachycardia (77%). Syncope (11%) also led to fewer management changes compared to hypoxia (57%). AMS triggered management changes in 79% of cases. Other triggers resulted in management changes 47% of the time. Hypotension/presyncope led to uptriaging in only 28% of patients. Syncope resulted in uptriaging 15% of the time. Hypoxia caused uptriaging in 30% of cases. Tachycardia resulted in significantly more uptriaging at 81% (P < .001). Hypotension/presyncope was found to be significantly more commonly due to volume depletion at 67% (P < .001). Hypoxia was significantly more commonly due to atelectasis in 57% of cases (P = .037). Opioids/oversedation caused hypoxia in 30.4% of patients. AMS/delirium was significantly more commonly caused by opioids/over-sedation at 71% (P < .001). The most common etiologies were potentially preventable through improved perioperative protocols and patient monitoring strategies.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::21: Emergency medical services play a critical role in managing acute stroke cases. In December 2006, we created the TOYOTA prehospital stroke scale for tissue plasminogen activator intravenous therapy (TOPSPIN) to identify patients requiring t-PA treatment. The scale evaluates five clinical parameters: consciousness level, presence of atrial fibrillation, language function, upper limb motor function, and lower limb motor function. This investigation assessed a decade of TOPSPIN application in distinguishing ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke under real-world conditions. From December 2006 through January 2017, we prospectively collected data on consecutive patients transported by Toyota city ambulance services who underwent TOPSPIN evaluation. The study analyzed final diagnoses at hospital discharge, including ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, and stroke mimics. We calculated the positive-predictive value for actual stroke cases among those screened. The proportion of patients receiving recanalization therapies was documented. Clinical characteristics distinguishing hemorrhagic stroke, ischemic stroke, and non-stroke conditions were identified. The cohort included 1,482 consecutive patients evaluated during the study period. Stroke was confirmed in 1,134 patients, representing 76.5% of the total sample. Within the stroke group, 628 had ischemic events, 34 experienced transient ischemic attacks, and 472 suffered hemorrhagic strokes. Non-stroke conditions accounted for 348 cases (23.5%), including 80 seizure patients, 42 syncope cases, 27 hypoglycemia episodes, and 199 miscellaneous diagnoses. Among the 628 ischemic stroke patients, 130 individuals (20.7%) underwent intravenous recombinant t-PA administration, endovascular intervention, or combined treatment approaches. Ischemic stroke patients more frequently demonstrated atrial fibrillation, advanced age, reduced blood pressure readings, and lower overall TOPSPIN scores compared to hemorrhagic stroke patients. Multivariable logistic regression modeling revealed that atrial fibrillation presence independently predicted ischemic stroke with an odds ratio of 2.33 (95% confidence interval 1.61-3.40). The TOPSPIN represents a practical prehospital assessment tool incorporating cardiac rhythm evaluation. Identifying atrial fibrillation during emergency transport suggests increased likelihood of ischemic rather than hemorrhagic stroke etiology.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::22: We aim to determine the redshift of GDS-1408, the most solid z~7 galaxy candidate lying in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field. We have used all the VLT spectra of GDS-1408 collected by us and two other groups with FORS2 at VLT in the last five years, for a total integration time of 52hr. The combined spectrum is the deepest ever obtained of a galaxy in the Reionization epoch. We do not detect any emission line or continuum over the whole wavelength range, up to 10100A. Based on an accurate set of simulations, we are able to put a stringent upper limit of f(Lya)<3x10^(-18) erg/s/cm2 at 3-9 sigma in the explored wavelength range. This flux limit corresponds to a rest-frame equivalent width EW<9A. Combining this limit with the SED modelling we refine the redshift to be z=6.82+/- 0.1 (1-sigma). The same SED fitting indicates that GDS-1408 is relatively extinct with A1600~1. The dust corrected star formation rate is estimated at approximately 20 Msol/yr. The case-B recombination theory predicts an un-attenuated equivalent width for this galaxy. The comparison between this theoretical prediction and the observed upper limit provides a limit on the effective Lya escape fraction of f_(esc)^(eff)(Lya)<8%. We cannot rule out a major contribution of the inter/circum galactic medium in damping the line. A plausible interpretation is that GDS-1408 is moderately evolved and contains sufficient gas and dust to attenuate the Lya emission before it reaches the intergalactic medium. The redshift confirmation of even the best z~7 candidates is very hard to achieve with the current generation of 8-10m class telescopes unless the Lya or unusually strong rest-UV nebular emission lines are present. We show that both JWST and E-ELT will be necessary to make decisive progresses in this field. Currently, the increased redshift accuracy obtained with this kind of analysis makes ALMA an interesting option for the redshift confirmation of high-redshift galaxy candidates. Future multi-wavelength campaigns will benefit from these complementary approaches.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::23: The survival of Salmonella spp. as pathogen indicator in composting was studied. The inoculums technique was used to gives the known amounts of Salmonella spp. involved in composting. Two different inoculation methods were compared to evaluate their effectiveness in pathogen elimination. Sample A received the Salmonella spp. solution added directly into the compost material, allowing immediate contact with the composting substrate. Sample B used the vial technique, where Salmonella spp. solution was placed into a sealed container and inserted into the middle of compost material before starting the composting process. The conventional method for enumeration involves serial dilution followed by standard membrane filtration as recommended in PAS 100 and British Standard (BS EN ISO 6579:2002). This study was designed to investigate the relationship of temperature and contact material that may also involve in pathogen activation specifically to Salmonella spp. Previous research by Deportes et al. (1995) reported that exposure to an average temperature during composting of about 55-60°C for at least 3 days sufficiently kills the vast majority of enteric pathogens. The amount of Salmonella spp. and temperature for both samples was set as indicator to determine the survival of Salmonella spp. in direct and non-direct inoculums. Quantitative die-off rates for Salmonella spp. during composting were calculated from the experimental data. The results from laboratory scale composting study showed that after 8 days at temperatures reaching at least 66°C, Sample A achieved Salmonella spp. numbers below the limits required by UK compost standard PAS 100 (BSI, 2005). The standard mandates that finished compost must be completely free of Salmonella spp. for commercial use. Sample B still contained high amounts of Salmonella spp. even after composting for 20 days, demonstrating the protective effect of the vial barrier. Direct contact with compost material proved essential for effective thermal inactivation of the pathogen. The physical barrier created by the vial prevented adequate heat transfer and limited exposure to antimicrobial compounds produced during composting.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::24: BACKGROUND: Although race is associated with prostate cancer progression in early stage disease, once men have advanced disease, it is unclear whether race continues to predict a poor outcome. The authors hypothesized that, in an equal-access setting among patients with castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) and no known metastases (M0/Mx), black men would receive imaging tests at similar rates as nonblack men (ie, there would be an equal opportunity to detect metastases) but would have a higher risk of metastatic disease. METHODS: In total, 837 men who were diagnosed with M0/Mx CRPC during 2000 through 2014 from 5 Veterans Affairs hospitals in the SEARCH (Shared Equal Access Regional Cancer Hospital) database were analyzed. Data on all imaging tests after CRPC diagnosis were collected, including date, type, and outcome. Multivariable Cox models were used to test associations between race and the time to first metastasis, first bone metastasis, first bone scan, second bone scan among men who had a negative first bone scan, and overall survival. RESULTS: Black men (n = 306) were equally as likely as nonblack men (n = 531) to receive a first and second bone scan after a diagnosis of CRPC. The risk of developing any metastases showed no statistically significant difference between the two racial groups. Bone metastases occurred at comparable rates regardless of race. Time intervals to receiving bone scans were similar across racial categories. Overall survival did not differ significantly by race in this cohort. All comparisons yielded P values exceeding .2, indicating no meaningful statistical differences. CONCLUSIONS: The lack of racial differences in the development of metastases and scanning practices observed in this study suggests that, once men have a diagnosis of M0/Mx CRPC, race may not be a prognostic factor. Efforts to understand prostate cancer racial disparities may derive greater benefit by focusing on the risk of developing prostate cancer and on the outcomes of men who have early stage disease. Cancer 2016;122:3848-3855. © 2016 American Cancer Society.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::25: We present deep Hubble Space Telescope single-star photometry of Leo A in B, V, and I filters. Our new field of view is offset from the centrally located field observed by Tolstoy et al. (1998) in order to expose the halo population of this galaxy. We report the detection of metal-poor red horizontal branch stars, which demonstrate that Leo A is not a young galaxy. Leo A is at least as old as metal-poor Galactic Globular Clusters which exhibit red horizontal branches. These particular clusters are considered to have a minimum age of about 9 Gyr. We discuss the distance to Leo A in our analysis. We perform an extensive comparison of the data with stellar isochrones to constrain stellar populations. For a distance modulus of 24.5, the data are better than 50% complete down to absolute magnitudes of 2 or more. We can easily identify stars with metallicities between 0.0001 and 0.0004 in the observations. Stars with ages between about 5 and 10 Gyr are detectable in their post-main-sequence phases. However, we lack the detection of main-sequence turnoffs which would provide unambiguous proof of ancient (>10 Gyr) stellar generations. Blue horizontal branch stars are above the detection limits of our observations. These blue stars are difficult to distinguish from young stars with similar colors and magnitudes. Synthetic color-magnitude diagrams show it is possible to populate the blue horizontal branch in the halo of Leo A. The models also suggest approximately 50% of the total astrated mass in our pointing should be attributed to an ancient (>10 Gyr) stellar population. We conclude that Leo A started to form stars at least about 9 Gyr ago based on multiple lines of evidence. Leo A exhibits an extremely low oxygen abundance, of only 3% of Solar, in its ionized interstellar medium. The existence of old stars in this very oxygen-deficient galaxy illustrates that a low oxygen abundance does not preclude a history of early star formation. This finding challenges assumptions about chemical enrichment requirements for primordial stellar populations.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::26: One goal of neuromorphic engineering is to create 'realistic' robotic systems that interact with the physical world by adopting neuromechanical principles from biology. Critical to this is the methodology to implement the spinal circuitry responsible for the behavior of afferented muscles. At its core, muscle afferentation is the closed-loop behavior arising from the interactions among populations of muscle spindle afferents, alpha and gamma motoneurons, and muscle fibers to enable useful behaviors. We used programmable very-large-scale-circuit (VLSI) hardware to implement simple models of spiking neurons, skeletal muscles, muscle spindle proprioceptors, alpha-motoneuron recruitment, gamma motoneuron control of spindle sensitivity, and the monosynaptic circuitry connecting them. The system emulated a pair of antagonistic afferented mammalian muscles acting on a joint via long tendons. Each muscle was simulated by 1024 alpha-motoneurones and 1024 gamma-motoneurones in the hardware implementation. The integrated system successfully maintained a joint angle during experimental trials. Stretch reflex responses were reproduced when the system drove the nonlinear biomechanics of an actual cadaveric finger. We explored numerous values and combinations of gamma-static and gamma-dynamic gains when driving a robotic finger. Some parameter combinations replicated specific human pathological conditions observed in clinical settings. We investigated the behavioral consequences of adopting three alternative models of isometric muscle force production. The dynamic responses to rate-coded spike trains produce force ramps that can be very sensitive to tendon elasticity. This sensitivity becomes especially pronounced at high force output levels. Our methodology produced the first example of an autonomous, multi-scale, neuromorphic, neuromechanical system capable of creating realistic reflex behavior in cadaveric fingers. This research platform allows exploration of mechanisms behind healthy sensorimotor function in the physical world by building them from first principles. The platform also enables investigation of pathological sensorimotor conditions through systematic manipulation of circuit parameters. The work serves as a precursor to fully autonomous neuromorphic robotic systems for real-world applications.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::27: Introduction and Objective: Patients presenting with a urinary tract infection combined with kidney or ureteral stones represent a urologic emergency requiring immediate intervention. These individuals typically stabilize quickly after initial treatment but must remain in the hospital pending urine antibiotic sensitivity test results. Our study sought to determine which clinical factors predict antibiotic resistance in patients requiring urgent urinary tract decompression for sepsis caused by obstructive urolithiasis. Such predictors could enable earlier hospital discharge with empiric oral antibiotic therapy. Methods: We retrospectively identified patients who received emergent urinary tract decompression for sepsis with an obstructing ureteral stone between 2014 and 2018. Two academic medical institutions provided the patient cohort for this investigation. All subjects underwent emergent ureteral stent placement as the decompression method. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics were administered to all enrolled patients following the procedure. We examined relationships between clinical parameters measured at initial presentation and the presence of resistance to at least one antibiotic detected in urine cultures. Statistical analysis employed the Wilcoxon test for continuous variables and Fisher exact test for categorical variables. Multivariate logistic regression incorporated all variables showing significance in the univariate analysis phase. Results: The final cohort comprised 134 patients meeting inclusion criteria. Urine cultures from 84 patients (62.7%) demonstrated resistance to at least one tested antibiotic agent. Univariate analysis revealed that patients harboring resistant organisms had significantly higher rates of previous ureteroscopy procedures. These same patients more frequently required postoperative intensive care unit-level monitoring. Bacteremia occurred more commonly in the resistant culture group. Hospital length of stay was significantly prolonged among patients with resistant infections. Multivariate analysis incorporating the significant univariate variables yielded only one independent predictor. Previous ureteroscopy remained the sole factor significantly associated with antibiotic resistance, conferring increased odds of 6.95 (p = 0.011). Conclusions: History of ureteroscopy represents a significant predictor of antibiotic resistance in this patient population across both analytical approaches. Clinical application suggests patients with prior ureteroscopy should await definitive culture results before discharge. Conversely, patients lacking ureteroscopy history may safely receive early discharge with empiric oral antibiotics. Prospective validation studies are needed to confirm this predictor's clinical utility.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::28: Evidence details how cannabis can influence the use of other psychoactive substances, including prescription medications, alcohol, tobacco and illicit drugs, but very little research has examined the factors associated with these changes in substance use patterns. This paper explores the self-reported use of cannabis as a substitute for alcohol among a Canadian medical cannabis patient population. Data was derived from a survey of 2102 people enrolled in the Canadian medical cannabis program. The analysis focused on 973 respondents, representing 44% of the total sample, who reported using alcohol on at least 10 occasions over a 12 month period prior to initiating medical cannabis. Retrospective data on the frequency and amount of alcohol use before and after medical cannabis initiation allowed researchers to determine which participant characteristics and other variables were associated with reductions and cessation of alcohol use. The study revealed that 419 participants, comprising 44% of the subsample, reported decreases in alcohol usage frequency over 30 days. Additionally, 323 participants, representing 34% of respondents, decreased the number of standard drinks they consumed per week. A smaller group of 76 participants, accounting for 8% of the sample, reported complete abstinence from alcohol in the 30 days prior to the survey. Participants below 55 years of age showed greater odds of reducing alcohol use compared to older respondents. Higher rates of alcohol consumption in the pre-medical cannabis period were also associated with increased likelihood of reduction. An explicit intention to use medical cannabis specifically to reduce alcohol consumption was associated with significantly greater odds of both reducing and ceasing alcohol use altogether. Alcohol remains the most prevalent recreational substance in North America. The use of alcohol results in significant rates of criminality, morbidity and mortality across the continent. These findings may lead to improved health outcomes for medical cannabis patients specifically. The results also suggest potential overall improvements in public health and safety at the population level.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::29: The delicate balance between spin-orbit coupling, Coulomb repulsion and crystalline electric field interactions observed in Ir-based oxides is usually manifested as exotic magnetic behavior. Here we investigate the evolution of the exchange coupling between Co and Ir for partial La substitution by Ca in La$_{2}$CoIrO$_6$. A great advantage of the use of Ca$^{2+}$ as replacement for La$^{3+}$ is the similarity of its ionic radii. Thus, the observed magnetic changes can more easily be associated to electronic variations. A thorough investigation of the structural, electronic and magnetic properties of the La$_{2-x}$Ca$_{x}$CoIrO$_6$ system was carried out by means of synchrotron x-ray powder diffraction, muon spin rotation and relaxation ($\mu$SR), AC and DC magnetization, XAS, XMCD, Raman spectroscopy, electrical resistivity and dielectric permittivity. Our XAS results show that up to 25% of Ca substitution at the La site results in the emergence of Co$^{3+}$, possibly in high spin state. The introduction of larger amounts of Ca beyond this threshold leads to the increase of Ir valence instead. The competing magnetic interactions resulting from the mixed valences lead to a coexistence of a magnetically ordered and an emerging spin glass (SG) state for the doped samples. Our $\mu$SR results indicate that for La$_{2}$CoIrO$_6$ a nearly constant fraction of a paramagnetic (PM) phase persists down to low temperature. This persistent PM behavior is possibly related to the presence of a small amount of Ir$^{3+}$ in the undoped parent compound. Anti-site disorder at Co/Ir sites may also contribute to the paramagnetic fraction observed. For the doped compounds the PM phase freezes below 30 K. Despite this freezing transition, there is still some dynamics associated with the SG phase at lower temperatures. The dielectric data obtained for the parent compound and the one with 25% of Ca-doping indicate a possible magnetodielectric effect. This coupling phenomenon is discussed in terms of the electron hopping between the TM ions. The anti-site disorder influences the magnetodielectric properties significantly. The distorted crystalline structure also plays a role in the observed magnetodielectric behavior.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::30: With the stringent requirements introduced by the new sixth-generation (6G) internet-of-things (IoT) use cases, traditional approaches to multiple access control have started to show their limitations. A new wave of grant-free (GF) approaches have been therefore proposed as a viable alternative. However, a definitive solution is still to be accomplished. In our work, we propose a new semi-GF coordinated random access (RA) protocol, denoted as partial-information multiple access (PIMA), to reduce packet loss and latency, particularly in the presence of sporadic activations. We consider a machine-type communications (MTC) scenario, wherein devices need to transmit data packets in the uplink to a base station (BS). When using PIMA, the BS can acquire partial information on the instantaneous traffic conditions. The base station employs compute-over-the-air techniques to estimate the number of devices with packets waiting for transmission in their queue. Based on this knowledge, the BS assigns to each device a single slot for transmission. Since each slot may still be assigned to multiple users, collisions may occur. Both the total number of allocated slots and the user assignments are optimized, based on the estimated number of active users, to reduce collisions. This optimization improves the efficiency of the multiple access scheme. To prove the validity of our solution, we compare PIMA to time-division multiple-access (TDMA) and slotted ALOHA (SALOHA) schemes. TDMA represents the ideal solution for orthogonal multiple access (OMA) in the time domain under low traffic conditions. SALOHA serves as the optimal approach when high traffic conditions prevail. We show that PIMA is able to adapt to different traffic conditions. The protocol provides fewer packet drops regardless of the intensity of packet generations. PIMA merges the advantages of both TDMA and SALOHA schemes. This combination delivers performance improvements in terms of packet loss probability. The system also achieves reduced latency compared to conventional methods.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::31: Background and purpose — Bone remodeling as a response to bone trauma, postoperative immobilization, and device-related bone reactions can lead to loss of bone stock and increase the risk of periprosthetic fracture and aseptic loosening. This study investigates the adaptive bone remodeling of the proximal tibia after uncemented total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Patients and methods — We performed a 2-year follow up of 53 patients with mean age 62 years, ranging from 38 to 70 years. The cohort included 27 male participants. All patients received an uncemented TKA in a randomized controlled trial with bone mineral density (BMD) as secondary endpoint. Randomization allocated patients to 2 groups of either monoblock (A) or modular (B) polyethylene design. The TKAs were performed using the uncemented Zimmer Nexgen trabecular metal. Measurements of BMD were done postoperatively and after 3, 6, 12, and 24 months. Three regions of interest (ROI) were defined for BMD measurement. Results and interpretation — In group A statistically significant changes in BMD were seen after 24 months in both the medial and lateral ROI. BMD decreased medially by 15% (p = 0.004). Lateral BMD decreased by 13% (p = 0.01). In group B the BMD changes were limited throughout the observation period. After 24 months group B returned to the preoperative values. The differences in BMD change between groups were statistically significant in both the medial (p = 0.03) and lateral (p = 0.02) ROI. In the distal ROI we found no significant change in BMD in either group. A significantly different bone remodeling pattern of the proximal tibia was seen in the 2 groups. A higher degree of bone loss occurred in the knees that received the monoblock polyethylene design. The flexible monoblock implant design had previously been shown to improve fixation. However, this design does not decrease the bone loss of the proximal tibia.
ideas_up_v2.academic_abstracts::32: Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are bio-inspired models of neural computation that have proven highly effective. ANNs lack a natural notion of time, which limits their biological plausibility. Neural units in ANNs exchange analog values in a frame-based manner, creating computational and energetic inefficiency.
